lead: An operational amplifier (op-amp) with negative feedback obeys two golden rules: no current enters its input terminals, and its two input terminals sit at almost the same voltage. Those rules turn a bare high-gain amplifier into precise building blocks. This chapter shows the voltage follower, adder, subtractor, integrator and comparator. A follower buffers a sensor; an adder and subtractor combine signals with resistors; an integrator uses one capacitor; a comparator uses no feedback and gives only two output levels. The same parts appear in sensor front ends, audio mixers, waveshaping and trip circuits.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.5, especially the virtual short rule and the saturation limits.

blocks.text: Voltage follower: connect the output directly to the inverting input, and drive the non-inverting input with Vin. Negative feedback forces V− = V+, so Vout = Vin. The gain is exactly 1. The input resistance is very high and the output resistance is very low, so the follower takes almost no current from a sensor and can drive a heavier load. Use it between a high-resistance sensor and a low-resistance load, or between stages.

Inverting adder: each input V1, V2, V3 goes through its own resistor R1, R2, R3 to the inverting input. Rf goes from output to that same input. The non-inverting input is grounded. Negative feedback and the virtual short make the inverting node a virtual ground, V− ≈ 0 V, while no current enters the op-amp input. Kirchhoff's current law at that node gives:

blocks.where: Vout is the output voltage in volts; V1, V2, V3 are input voltages in volts; R1, R2, R3 are input resistors in ohms; Rf is the feedback resistor in ohms.

blocks.text: With equal input resistors R and Rf = R/N for N inputs, the output is the negative average. With Rf = R, the output is the negative sum. The minus sign comes from the inverting input.

A non-inverting adder feeds the inputs through equal resistors to V+. With equal input resistors the non-inverting input sits at the average (V1 + V2 + … + VN)/N, so Vout = (1 + Rf/R1) × average, positive and with no minus sign.

A difference amplifier subtracts two voltages. V1 goes through R1 to the inverting input; Rf is the feedback resistor from output to that input. V2 goes through R2 to the non-inverting input; R3 connects that input to ground. Set Rf/R1 = R3/R2. The circuit is balanced. Then the output is:

blocks.where: Vout is the output voltage in volts; V1 and V2 are input voltages in volts; Rf, R1, R2 and R3 are resistors in ohms.

blocks.text: R1 and Rf set the gain; R2 and R3 divide V2 by the same factor. If the resistor ratios are not equal, V2 is scaled differently from V1; the circuit amplifies common-mode voltage and rejects less. In the balanced case, a common voltage on both inputs gives zero output. Difference amplifiers read a small voltage between two sensor wires while rejecting noise that appears on both. A common use is the front end of an ECG or a current-sense circuit.

Swap the feedback resistor Rf for a capacitor C. The input resistor is R1. The inverting node stays at virtual ground. The current through R1 is Vin/R1. That current charges C. With the sign of the inverting input, the output is:

blocks.where: Vout(t) is the output voltage in volts at time t; Vout(0) is the output voltage at t = 0 (0 V in the worked figure); Vin is the input voltage in volts; R1 is the input resistor in ohms; C is the feedback capacitor in farads; t is time in seconds; ∫₀ᵗ Vin dt is in volt-seconds; R1C is the time constant in seconds.

blocks.text: The output changes at a slope of −Vin/(R1C). A constant positive input gives a falling ramp; a constant negative input gives a rising ramp. A square wave therefore becomes a triangle wave. If the input is +1 V for 1 ms and R1C = 1 ms, the slope is −1000 V/s, so the output falls by 1 V in 1 ms. A sine becomes a cosine scaled by 1/(ωR1C), with no extra minus sign in the result: Vout = (A/(ωR1C))cos(ωt) for Vin = A sin(ωt). The only minus sign is the one already inside the formula Vout = −(1/(R1C))∫Vin dt. The differentiator is the mirror: capacitor C at input, resistor R in feedback, giving Vout = −RC dVin/dt. It responds to edges and is noisy, so practical versions add a small input resistor.

A comparator uses the op-amp without feedback. The output cannot settle between the rails; it hits near +Vsat or −Vsat. Vsat is the saturation voltage, a little below the supply voltage. With Vin on V+ and a reference Vref on V−, Vout is high when Vin > Vref and low when Vin < Vref. This is a level detector. With Vref = 0 V it is a zero-crossing detector: the output changes state each time the input crosses 0 V. It is used to convert a slow analog signal into a clean logic edge, in trip circuits and in zero-crossing dimmers.

A Schmitt trigger adds positive feedback from output to V+. It has two thresholds: an upper threshold VUT and a lower threshold VLT. The output switches high only after the input rises above VUT, and low only after it falls below VLT. The gap VUT − VLT is the hysteresis. Hysteresis stops a noisy input near one threshold from making many fast output changes. The 555 timer uses two such levels internally; see Chapter 4.7.

figure.caption: A ±1 V square wave of 1 ms half period drives an integrator with R1C = 1 ms. The output is a triangle: it falls while the input is high and rises while the input is low.

spec.aria: Plot of an integrator fed with a ±1 V square wave of 1 ms half period: the output is a triangle wave falling while the input is high and rising while it is low.

examples.question: An inverting adder has Rf = 20 kΩ and three input resistors of 10 kΩ each, fed with V1 = 1 V, V2 = 2 V and V3 = 0.5 V. Supplies are ±12 V. Find Vout and the current through Rf.
steps: The non-inverting input is grounded, so the virtual short gives V− ≈ 0 V at the inverting node.
Current through R1: I1 = V1/R1 = 1 V / 10 kΩ = 0.10 mA.
Current through R2: I2 = V2/R2 = 2 V / 10 kΩ = 0.20 mA.
Current through R3: I3 = V3/R3 = 0.5 V / 10 kΩ = 0.05 mA.
Total current into the node: I = I1 + I2 + I3 = 0.10 + 0.20 + 0.05 = 0.35 mA. This current flows through Rf.
Output: Vout = 0 − I × Rf = −0.35 mA × 20 kΩ = −7 V.
The supply is ±12 V, and −7 V lies between the rails, so the op-amp does not saturate.
Current through Rf = 0.35 mA, the same as the total input current.
examples.answer: Vout = −7 V and the current through Rf is 0.35 mA.
examples.check:
Rf = 20e3
R1 = R2 = R3 = 10e3
V1, V2, V3 = 1.0, 2.0, 0.5
I1 = V1 / R1
I2 = V2 / R2
I3 = V3 / R3
I_sum = I1 + I2 + I3
Vout = -Rf * I_sum
I_Rf = abs(Vout) / Rf
print(Vout)
print(I_Rf * 1000)

traps: Forgetting the minus sign in the inverting adder or integrator. The input goes to the inverting input, so Vout is negative for positive inputs.
Thinking a comparator is a linear amplifier. With no feedback there is no virtual short; the output is only near +Vsat or −Vsat.
Using the balanced difference-amplifier formula when Rf/R1 ≠ R3/R2. Then V2 is scaled differently and common-mode rejection is poor.
Mixing up average and sum in an adder. Equal input resistors R with Rf = R give the negative sum; for N inputs the negative average needs Rf = R/N.
Forgetting the unit of R1C in the integrator. R1 in ohms times C in farads gives seconds; the slope is volts per second.

quiz.q: State the voltage gain of a voltage follower and one reason to use it.
quiz.a: Gain = 1, so Vout = Vin. It gives high input resistance and low output resistance, so it buffers a sensor from a load.

quiz.q: Why is the inverting input of an inverting adder called a virtual ground?
quiz.a: Negative feedback keeps V− almost equal to V+ = 0 V. It is not physically grounded, but it sits near 0 V and draws no input current.

quiz.q: A difference amplifier has Rf = 20 kΩ, R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R3 = 20 kΩ, V1 = 1 V and V2 = 3 V. Find Vout.
quiz.a: Rf/R1 = 2 and R3/R2 = 2, so it is balanced. Vout = (20/10)(3 − 1) = 4 V.

quiz.q: An integrator has R1 = 10 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF. Vin = 1 V is held for 2 ms. Find the change in Vout.
A comparator has +Vsat = 12 V, −Vsat = −12 V, Vref = 2 V. Vin is a 1 kHz sine of amplitude 5 V. Describe the output.
quiz.a: Output is about +12 V while Vin > 2 V and about −12 V while Vin < 2 V. It is a rectangular wave at 1 kHz, not a scaled sine; the duty cycle is less than 50%.

quiz.q: Why does a Schmitt trigger not switch rapidly when the input has noise near a threshold?
quiz.a: Positive feedback gives two thresholds. After a switch, the input must pass the other threshold to switch back, so small noise near one level cannot toggle the output repeatedly.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the same golden rules build instrumentation amplifiers that read a thermocouple or a strain gauge, active filters that shape a signal before an ADC, and precision rectifiers that beat the 0.7 V diode drop. Analog computers used integrators and adders to solve differential equations; today small integrators appear in ramp generators and charge amplifiers. Search next for instrumentation amplifier, active low-pass filter, precision rectifier, and Schmitt trigger hysteresis.
